title: The hidden depths of the Gospels
source_text: Καὶ οὔπω λέγω περὶ τῆς ἐν τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις τηρήσεως πάντων τῶν γεγραμμένων· ὧν ἕκαστον πολὺν καὶ δυσθεώρητον οὐ μόνον τοῖς πολλοῖς ἀλλὰ καὶ τισι τῶν συνετῶν περιέχει λόγον. ἔχοντα διήγησιν βαθυτάτην παραβολῶν, ὧν τοῖς „ἔξω“ ἐλάλησεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς, τηρῶν αὐτῶν τὴν σαφήνειαν τοῖς ὑπερβεβηκόσι τὰς ἐξωτερικὰς ἀκοὰς καὶ κατ᾿ ἰδίαν αὐτῷ „ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ“ προσερχομένοις, θαυμάσεται δὲ νοήσας, τίνα λόγον ἔχει τὸ „ἔξω“ τινὰς ὀνομάζεσθαι καὶ ἄλλους „ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ.“ καὶ πάλιν τίς οὐκ ἂν καταπλαγείη τῶν δυναμένων βλέπειν τὰς Ἰησοῦ μεταβάσεις, ἀναβαίνοντος μὲν εἰς ὄρος ἐπὶ τοιοῖσδε λόγοις ἢ πράξεσιν ἢ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ μεταμορφώσει. κάτω δὲ θεραπεύοντος τοὺς ἀσθενοῦντας καὶ μὴ δυναμένους ἀναβαίνειν ὅπου ἕπονται αὐτῷ οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ; διηγεῖσθαι δὲ νῦν τὰ ἀληθῶς σεμνὰ καὶ θεῖα τῶν εὐαγγελίων ἢ τὸν ἐν τῷ Παύλῳ Χριστοῦ. τουτέστι τῆς σοφίας καὶ τοῦ λόγου, νοῦν οὐκ εὔκαιρον. ἀλλ᾿ αὐτάρκη καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς τὴν ἀφιλόσοφον χλεύην τοῦ Κέλσου. ὁμοιοῦντος τὰ ἔνδον καὶ μυστικὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας τοῦ θεοῦ τοῖς Αἰγυπτίων αἰλούροις ἢ πιθήκοις ἢ κροκοδείλοις ἢ τράγοις ἢ κυσίν.
pass_a_gloss: And I do not yet speak about the careful observation/study (τήρησις) in the Gospels of all the things written; each of which contains (περιέχει) much and hard-to-contemplate (δυσθεώρητον) meaning (λόγον), not only for the many but even for some of the intelligent (συνετῶν), [a meaning] having a most profound explanation (διήγησιν βαθυτάτην) of parables (παραβολαί), which Jesus spoke to those 'outside' (ἔξω), keeping (τηρῶν) their clarity (σαφήνεια) for those who had passed beyond (ὑπερβεβηκόσι) the outer hearings (ἐξωτερικὰς ἀκοάς) and approached (προσερχομένοις) him privately (κατ᾿ ἰδίαν) 'in the house' (ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ); and he will marvel, having understood, what reason there is that some are named 'outside' and others 'in the house'. And again, who of those able to see would not be astounded (καταπλαγείη) at the passings (μεταβάσεις) of Jesus, going up into a mountain (ὄρος) for such-and-such words or deeds or for his own transfiguration (μεταμόρφωσις), but below (κάτω) healing (θεραπεύοντος) those who are sick (ἀσθενοῦντας) and unable to go up where his disciples follow him? But to narrate now the truly solemn and divine things (σεμνὰ καὶ θεῖα) of the Gospels, or the mind of Christ in Paul, that is, of the Wisdom (σοφία) and of the Word (λόγος), is not timely (οὐκ εὔκαιρον). But these things too are sufficient (αὐτάρκη) against the unphilosophical (ἀφιλόσοφον) mockery (χλεύη) of Celsus, likening (ὁμοιοῦντος) the inner and mystical things of the Church of God (ἐκκλησία τοῦ θεοῦ) to the cats or apes or crocodiles or goats or dogs of the Egyptians.

lemmas.lemma: τὸν ἐν τῷ Παύλῳ Χριστοῦ νοῦν

pass_b_english: And I say nothing yet of the close study of everything written in the Gospels, each part of which holds a meaning that is large and hard to discern, not only for the many but even for some of the intelligent. That meaning contains a most profound explanation of the parables, which Jesus spoke to “those outside” (Mark 4:11), while he kept their clear sense for those who had passed beyond outward hearing and came to him privately (Mark 4:34) “in the house” (Matthew 13:36). And he will marvel when he understands why some are called “outside” and others “in the house.”

And again, who among those able to see would not be struck with wonder at Jesus’ movements: going up a mountain for certain words (Matthew 5:1), or deeds, or for his own transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–2), and below healing those who were sick and unable to go up where his disciples follow him (Matthew 17:14–18)? But now is not the time to set out what is truly solemn and divine in the Gospels, or the mind of Christ in Paul (1 Corinthians 2:16), that is, of Wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24) and of the Word. But even these remarks are enough against the unphilosophical mockery of Celsus, who likens the inner and mystical things of the Church of God to the cats, or apes, or crocodiles, or goats, or dogs of the Egyptians.

choices.choice: The full stop printed after λόγον is treated as a comma: ἔχοντα agrees with λόγον, so the 'meaning' is what contains the explanation of the parables. The subject of θαυμάσεται ('he will marvel') carries on from the end of 3.20: the critic who reads with attention. Mark 4:11 has ἐκείνοις δὲ τοῖς ἔξω ἐν παραβολαῖς τὰ πάντα γίνεται; 'privately' (κατ᾿ ἰδίαν) echoes Mark 4:34; 'in the house' with the disciples approaching (προσῆλθον αὐτῷ) is Matthew 13:36, where Jesus explains the parable of the weeds; Mark 7:17 is a parallel. Mountain and descent: Matthew 5:1 (going up the mountain to teach), Matthew 17:1-2 (μετεμορφώθη, the transfiguration) and Matthew 17:14-18 (on coming down, the healing of the boy the disciples could not heal); these are allusions to a pattern rather than quotations, chosen as the clearest instances; Matthew 8:1-4 (healing after coming down) is also possible. 'The mind of Christ' (νοῦς Χριστοῦ) is 1 Corinthians 2:16; Christ as Wisdom is 1 Corinthians 1:24, and as Word recalls John 1:1 (not cited inline because Origen names the title, not the verse). Wisdom and Word are capitalised because they name Christ. The full stops after Κέλσου and after εὔκαιρον are treated as commas. Mark 4:34 (κατ᾿ ἰδίαν δὲ τοῖς ἰδίοις μαθηταῖς ἐπέλυεν πάντα) is now cited inline beside 'privately', since Origen's 'keeping their clear sense for those who came to him privately' is that verse's point. 1 Corinthians 1:24 names Christ as God's Wisdom only, so the citation now sits beside 'Wisdom', not after 'Word'.
νοῦν οὐκ εὔκαιρον: 'would not be timely' (conditional added) -> 'now is not the time'
τὸν ... Χριστοῦ, τουτέστι τῆς σοφίας καὶ τοῦ λόγου, νοῦν: dropped repeated 'the mind' -> 'that is, of Wisdom and of the Word'

Mark 4:11, Mark 4:34, Matthew 13:36 (προσῆλθον αὐτῷ in the house), Matthew 5:1, 17:1-2, 17:14-18, 1 Corinthians 2:16, 1:24 checked; mountain/descent citations are the clearest instances of a pattern, alternatives in notes
